query: As-cast HfMoTaTiZr has high strength at room temperature and elevated temperature but a relatively high density of 10.21 g cm−3. What single intervention could reduce its density without sacrificing its mechanical properties at room temperature and at elevated temperatures, including approximately 1000 °C? State the proposed intervention and mechanism, predict directional changes relative to as-cast HfMoTaTiZr, define the applicable temperature and loading boundaries, identify supporting prior evidence, and propose an experiment and rejection criterion that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Replacing the heavy element Ta with a lighter refractory element Nb in as‐cast HfMoTaTiZr (resulting in a HfMoNbTiZr alloy) will reduce the overall density while retaining comparable high‐temperature and room-temperature mechanical strength.
generation.material_initial_state: As‐cast HfMoTaTiZr high-entropy alloy with a density of approximately 10.21 g/cm³ and high strength at room temperature and around 1000 °C.
generation.intervention: Substitute Ta with Nb to form HfMoNbTiZr.
generation.conditions: Mechanical testing under room temperature conditions and at elevated temperatures (up to approximately 1000 °C) using tensile and/or creep experiments, under similar casting and cooling conditions as the original alloy.
generation.structural_mediator: Maintenance of similar phase stability and microstructure (for example, a BCC or dual-phase structure) due to the comparable atomic radii and refractory nature of Nb relative to Ta, which helps preserve fine grain sizes and dislocation barriers.
generation.mechanism: By replacing Ta (which is very heavy) with Nb (a lighter refractory element that still exhibits high melting point and strength), the overall density decreases. Nb can maintain the high-temperature stability and the dislocation/precipitation strengthening mechanisms that are critical to the alloy’s performance, thus preserving mechanical properties while reducing mass.
generation.predicted_outcome: The modified HfMoNbTiZr alloy should have a lower density (potentially reducing the overall density by roughly 5–10%) compared with the original alloy, with room temperature and ~1000 °C mechanical properties closely matching those of as-cast HfMoTaTiZr.
generation.baseline: As-cast HfMoTaTiZr performance: ~10.21 g/cm³ density with high strength maintained from room temperature to ~1000 °C.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies to as-cast, vacuum-melted, and similarly cooled high-entropy alloys tested under static and creep loading in the range 25 °C to ~1000 °C. It presumes that the substitution does not inadvertently promote deleterious secondary phase formation that would affect long-term performance.
generation.uncertainty: Exact quantitative retention of mechanical strength and long-term high-temperature creep resistance is uncertain, as phase stability (and any subtle changes in precipitation behavior) following the substitution may differ slightly under prolonged exposure or cyclic loading conditions. Additional uncertainty exists regarding any changes in oxidation resistance at high temperature.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize the HfMoNbTiZr alloy using an identical as-cast process to that used for HfMoTaTiZr. Characterize the microstructure using X-ray diffraction (XRD) and scanning electron microscopy (SEM) to ensure that the desired phases and grain structures are maintained. Measure the density using Archimedes’ method. Conduct room temperature tensile tests and high-temperature creep tests (around 1000 °C) under equivalent loads to assess mechanical performance.
measurements: Microstructural features (grain size, secondary phase distribution) via SEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the HfMoNbTiZr alloy does not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in density compared to 10.21 g/cm³, or if its room temperature or high-temperature (approx. 1000 °C) mechanical strengths are reduced by more than about 10% relative to HfMoTaTiZr, or if undesirable phase transformations emerge that compromise performance, then the hypothesis is falsified.

System: Ta20Nb20Hf20Zr20Ti20 (equiatomic atomic percentages). Processing: Vacuum arc melting (4 re-melts), casting into bars (gravity or suction-assisted), followed by Hot Isostatic Pressing (HIP) at 1230 °C and 152 MPa for 4 h. Test conditions: Room temperature tensile tests, compression tests at room temperature, and creep tests at 982 °C under 200 MPa and 120 MPa loads.
